title: The Distribution and the CDF
quickIdea: One function answers every probability question about a single variable: F(x) = P(X <= x), the cumulative distribution function. For a discrete variable it is a staircase, for a continuous one it is a smooth curve.
remember: F(x) = P(X <= x) is defined for every real x, not only for the values X takes.
For a discrete variable F is a staircase: it is flat between values and jumps at each value x by exactly P(X = x). F(-1) in the 2012 question is 0.5, not 0.
For a continuous variable with density f, F is continuous and F'(x) = f(x) wherever F is differentiable.
Three properties always hold: F is non-decreasing, F(x) tends to 0 as x tends to minus infinity and to 1 as x tends to plus infinity, and F is right-continuous.
Interval probabilities: P(a < X <= b) = F(b) - F(a). For a continuous X the strict and weak inequalities give the same number.
The CDF determines the distribution completely: a distribution can be written as a table, a formula or a CDF, and the three carry the same information.

example.prompt: X takes the values +1 and -1 with probability 0.5 each. Find F(-2), F(-1), F(0) and F(1).
example.work: F(-2) = P(X <= -2) = 0 because -2 is below every value. F(-1) = P(X <= -1) = P(X = -1) = 0.5, since the jump happens at -1 and the definition uses <=. F(0) = P(X <= 0) = 0.5, because nothing sits between -1 and 0. F(1) = P(X <= 1) = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1, and F stays 1 to the right of 1.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2012 Q.21 is exactly this computation, and its distractor 0 and 0.5 is what you get by reading the jump as belonging to the next point. Whenever a question gives a CDF and asks for a probability, the operation is subtraction: F(b) - F(a).

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2012 Q.21: X takes +1 and -1 with probability 0.5 each. The values of F(x) at x = -1 and x = +1 are (A) 0 and 0.5 (B) 0 and 1 (C) 0.5 and 1 (D) 0.25 and 0.75.
variations.why: F(-1) = P(X <= -1) = 0.5 includes the mass at -1 itself; F(1) = P(X <= 1) = 1 adds the mass at +1. Option (A) comes from using < instead of <=, which is the whole point of the question.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: For x >= 0 a variable has F(x) = 1 - e^(-2x), and F(x) = 0 for x < 0. Find P(1 < X <= 2) and the density at x = 1.
variations.why: Subtract the CDF: F(2) - F(1) = (1 - e^(-4)) - (1 - e^(-2)). The density is the derivative, F'(x) = 2 e^(-2x), evaluated at 1. This is the exponential family, and it is the same CDF the 2021 question uses in the form P(X > x) = e^(-lambda x).

trap.what: Using the strict inequality for a discrete variable, or assuming F is continuous when the variable is discrete.
trap.why: The definition is P(X <= x). At a point where mass sits, the two readings differ by exactly that mass, which is usually one of the printed options.
trap.counterexample: For the 2012 variable, P(X < -1) = 0 while P(X <= -1) = 0.5. Writing the first as F(-1) gives option (A) 0 and 0.5, which is the trap the question is built around.

check.question: A CDF is F(x) = 0 for x < 0, F(x) = x/4 for 0 <= x < 4, and F(x) = 1 for x >= 4. What is P(1 < X <= 3)?
check.explanation: F(3) - F(1) = 3/4 - 1/4 = 0.5. The variable is continuous and uniform on (0, 4), so the answer is also the length 2 divided by the total length 4.
